Source: https://dvolcore.github.io/futures-friends/. This is plain text copied from the public pages; the private curriculum is not part of it. Each section starts with its web address.

Booker

The Brave Little Learner

Early literacy, storytelling, listening, and the courage to try again.

Try one tonight: Brave Reader Steps
5 minutes, cozy spot, nothing to buy

Draw a sun, a cat and a kite, and write the word under each: SUN, CAT, KITE.
Start with CAT. Point to each letter and say its sound, /k/ /a/ /t/, then blend: "cat."
Hold up KITE and look at all four letters. Say, "In kite, the quiet e helps i say its name." Slide a finger under the word: /k/ /ī/ /t/, then blend: "kite."
Talk about the picture and what the word means. Then do the brave cheer and try SUN.
See Brave Reader Steps in the family library
Meet the friends and their books

Each statement and profile was supplied by the professional for Futures Learning Center. They are reviews of the curriculum and the menu, not an accreditation or a certification of every recipe.

Who is with your child, and how we know they are ready

The law sets the minimum before any teacher is alone with children. Our training is designed to add mastery and proof on the job, and we tell you exactly where it stands.

Before day one
Background checks, orientation and safety training, by state law
100% on life-safety
Rest-time supervision, reporting and missing-child questions, every time
Seen in the room
A director checklist within 30 days of each course

Our courses are in development and not yet approved by either state.

## Booker, Lumi, Zuri and Bop
https://dvolcore.github.io/futures-friends/friends

Friends & Books
FRIENDS AND BOOKS
Booker, Lumi, Zuri and Bop

Four plush-and-felt friends share the Clubhouse. Each looks after one learning pillar and practices one value.

Booker
The Brave Little Learner
LEARN
Confidence

Early literacy, storytelling, listening, and the courage to try again.

Zone: Booker's Reading Area

Lumi
The Kindness Keeper
BELONG
Kindness

Naming feelings, calming down, friendship and making room for everyone.

Zone: Lumi's Calm Corner

Zuri
The Curious Explorer
EXPLORE
Curiosity

Questions, nature, numbers, shapes and simple experiments.

Zone: Zuri's Discovery Zone

Bop
The Mighty Mover
MOVE
Independence

Movement, music, routines, clean-up and doing it myself.

Zone: Bop's Movement Zone

: Brave Reader Steps
Brave Reader Steps
39 seconds · story-world animation
Look at the picture, then at every letter: slide your finger under k-i-t-e and say /k/ /ī/ /t/ (the quiet e helps i say its name). Not quite? Big breath, brave heart, try again.
Activity card: try it together →

STORY-WORLD CHARACTER

Supporting-character illustration previews, adapted from the supplied model guides. Everyone in town is a story-world character.

Four finished covers

The revised editions of October 2026: each friend's book with its finished story-world art. Tap a cover to read it.

Booker Tries Again
Book 1 · A story about practice and asking for help
Lumi’s Big Feelings, Brighter Days
Book 2 · A story about noticing, listening, and inviting
Zuri: What Happens If We Try?
Book 3 · A story about ice, water, and wondering
Bop’s Clean-Up Team
Book 4 · A story about small steps and helping together

Every word of all five stories is free to read now in Story Time. Printed editions are not available yet.

Five stories, free to read

Picture books for ages 2 to 5, each with a say-along refrain, a Talk About It page and a five-minute activity. Read them free in Story Time; 8.5 by 8.5 inch printed editions are planned.

Booker Tries Again
Finished cover
Illustrated · 18 pages
LEARN · Confidence

Booker finds a new book with a word he does not know yet. Lumi helps him look at all four letters of k-i-t-e, where the quiet e helps i say its name, and they read it together. Then Booker welcomes his little sister into story time before she can read.

Lumi’s Big Feelings, Brighter Days
Finished cover
Illustrated · 18 pages
BELONG · Kindness

Lumi notices Pip, the new little hedgehog, standing quietly by the fence during the Parade game. Instead of deciding how Pip feels, she asks. A slow breath helps her feel ready even with a wobbly tummy, and a kind invitation, at Pip's own pace, brightens Pip's day.

Zuri: What Happens If We Try?
Finished cover
Illustrated · 18 pages
EXPLORE · Curiosity

An ice cube disappears from the sunny porch, leaving only a puddle. Zuri and her friends make guesses, set up three ice cubes about the same size, and watch closely: ice melts when it gets warm enough, and water freezes when it gets cold enough. No winner, just what they saw, and a brand-new question.

Bop’s Clean-Up Team
Finished cover
Illustrated · 18 pages
MOVE · Independence

After a big morning of play, Bop sees the biggest mess in the Clubhouse. He starts with one small thing, tries again when the books slide down, lends Zuri a hand (and a trunk), and the whole clean-up team finishes the job together.

The Rainbow Picnic
The Rainbow Picnic
Layout preview
40 planned pages
All four friends

Nana Hoot asks the friends to make a rainbow lunch, one food for every color. Booker reads the recipe, Zuri explores the garden, Bop does the heavy lifting, and Lumi makes room for everyone. When a rain cloud rolls in, they find out what they can do together.

The four friends' books are the revised, illustrated editions (October 2026), read free in Story Time page by page. The Rainbow Picnic's pictures are still a layout, and printed editions are not available yet.

Read all five stories free in Story Time

Thirteen short episodes, one a week, each with a talk-about-it card for grown-ups. They are written and outlined in the Futures Friends Series Bible; none has been made yet.

What we hold ourselves to

Futures Learning Center is where the Futures Friends program runs first. Everything we teach is meant to be tested here first, with real children and real families.

1
Curriculum-based care

Lessons for twos, threes and pre-K, planned as twelve monthly units with a readiness checklist before kindergarten. Eleven of the twelve months are written day by day as drafts, and none is approved yet.

2
Purposeful play

Four learning zones, outdoor time twice a day, music, cooking and art. It looks like play because it is; the teacher knows what each activity is for.

3
Teacher connection

Small groups in Missouri ratios, Futures Friends Academy training as its courses are ready, and a daily update in the Family App once the Futures Hub is live.

What a day looks like

A sample day in the Threes Room; times are a sample, so ask us for the current schedule. Every room follows the same rhythm, adjusted for age.

Planned design
Real room
With the kit
A classroom at Futures Learning Center: a table with learning trays, a chalkboard easel and the days of the week on the wall.
Planned design.
Planned design: the Futures Friends Learning Zones kit in our classroom (Zuri's Discovery Zone added; not installed yet).
Photo: Futures Learning Center, Independence, Missouri
7:00
Arrival and free choice
A teacher greets your child at the door and you sign in; children choose a learning zone while friends arrive. Tablet sign-in comes with the app pilot.
8:00
Breakfast
Family-style breakfast from the Eat the Rainbow menu, served at child-sized tables.
8:45
Circle time and episode
Songs and the friend of the week. Short Futures Friends episodes join circle time once they are finished; none is yet.
9:15
Learning zones
Reading, Calm Corner, Discovery and Movement zones, with a teacher-led small group.
10:30
Outdoor play
Climbing, running, gardening and nature detective walks, weather permitting.
11:30
Lunch
A hot lunch planned around the CACFP meal pattern. Children serve themselves with help and are invited to look at, smell or taste one new color. Saying no thanks is fine.
12:30
Rest time
Lights low, soft music and a blanket from home. Quiet books for early risers.
2:30
Snack
A rainbow snack and water, then a story with Booker.
3:00
Afternoon zones and outdoor time
Art, building, music and a second outdoor block.
4:30
Pickup
A teacher tells you about the day and gives you one question to ask at dinner. The Family App daily update comes with the app pilot.
A DAY HERE
How the day works, from arrival to pickup

Each practice is marked until the center confirms it for this year.

Arrival
Owner to confirm
A teacher greets each child at the door and you sign your child in. Children choose a learning zone while friends arrive. Tablet sign-in comes with the app pilot.
Meals
Owner to confirm
Breakfast, lunch and an afternoon snack are included, planned around the USDA CACFP meal pattern and served family-style. Tasting is always the child’s choice.
Rest
Owner to confirm
Rest time after lunch with lights low; a blanket from home is welcome. Quiet books for children who wake early.
Outdoor play
Owner to confirm
Outdoor time twice a day, weather permitting.
Pickup
Owner to confirm
A teacher tells you about the day and gives you one question to ask at dinner.
Communication
Owner to confirm
Talk with your child’s teacher at drop-off and pickup, or call (816) 988-5661. The Family App’s daily update comes with the app pilot.
Transitions
Owner to confirm
One friendly cue moves the room from one activity to the next, so children know what comes next without raised voices.

Prepare breakfast, lunch and snack designed around the CACFP meal pattern for the whole center, following each child's director-approved meal instruction.

See open positions
Floater and Substitute

Cover breaks and absences across rooms so every room stays in ratio.

See open positions
Why teach at Futures
Full time, Monday to Friday, no weekends
Paid time for Level 1 Foundations training once its courses are ready (in development)
A planned path to Level 2, Level 3 and Director levels (Futures Friends levels, not state credentials)
Training courses being prepared for Missouri and Kansas review; their hours count toward required annual hours only once approved
Small groups in Missouri ratios, with a floater for breaks
Background screening through the Missouri Family Care Safety Registry is required for all staff

PARTNER-CENTER PACKAGE
What a licensed center gets

A licensable operating system, not a folder of PDFs. Six parts that work together so families see one consistent program.

MEDIA
Episodes, songs and clips.
CURRICULUM
Weekly guide, activities and age adaptations.
ENVIRONMENT
Posters, rug, zones and signage.
FAMILY
Take-home pages, the pickup prompt and the home challenge.
TRAINING
Onboarding and an implementation standard.
MERCH
Optional plush, books and kits.

ONE LICENSE. ONE CONSISTENT FAMILY EXPERIENCE ACROSS LOCATIONS.

This is a proposed partner package. Scope and terms are confirmed in a conversation. See the published program pricing, or learn how the day works on the whole-child page.

HOW IT WORKS FOR PARTNERS
Four engines that reinforce each other

The childcare operation creates the audience. The characters and the shared program expand what a center can offer.

1
Childcare

Your center starts it all.

Tuition, enrollment and retention. A program families can see on every tour and at every pickup gives your center something recognizable to talk about.

2
Media and IP

Children meet the friends on screen.

Books, episodes, music and digital. Children meet the friends in stories, then find them in your classroom.

3
Products

Characters children already love.

Plush, kits, books and learning tools. Optional, child-facing products extend the rituals children already know.

4
Licensing

One program across locations.

Center package, training and renewals. The same characters, language and routines in every location you run.

ENROLLMENT
→
CHARACTER ATTACHMENT
→
PRODUCT DEMAND
→
LICENSING

We do not promise enrollment or revenue results. That is why the plan starts with a pilot.

PILOT BEFORE SCALE
Prove it in a real center first

Our plan is to validate engagement, teacher workload and parent value before expanding the catalog.

1
Lock
Finalize pillar kits and parent language.
2
Pilot
Run it in one Futures center.
3
Measure
Observe children, teachers and parents.
4
Refine
Fix friction before productizing.
5
Scale
More centers, then a licensing pilot.

Trying counts here
Rewards
Friendship Stars

A star card from one of the friends for trying again, helping out, asking a question or finishing the puzzle a child nearly quit.

Exploring new foods
Food explorer talk

Look, smell, touch and describe new foods at the table. Tasting is always the child's choice, and nothing is charted or rewarded.

Community
Friday circle

On Friday the class sits together and names who showed the week's value. The news goes home to families.

Four zones, open all day
Booker's Reading Area
Early literacy, storytelling, listening, and the courage to try again.
Lumi's Calm Corner
Naming feelings, calming down, friendship and making room for everyone.
Zuri's Discovery Zone
Questions, nature, numbers, shapes and simple experiments.
Bop's Movement Zone
Movement, music, routines, clean-up and doing it myself.
Twos, pre-K and everyone in between
Age versions

Every activity has a simpler version for twos and a stretch for pre-K.

Observe and adapt

Learning Steps help teachers notice what each child is doing and what comes next.

Language support

Picture cards and key words for English learners.

Futures Include

Classroom adaptations and early intervention guidance, alongside the curriculum. The Futures Hub does not store IEP or IFSP goals or health records.

Sample data
Director, "What's due": each item names the state rule it comes from, with an inspection binder to print. Screenshot of the preview with made-up children and staff. How the Futures Hub works
Ages 2 to 5, in three age bands

Twelve units, forty-eight theme weeks, with versions for twos, threes and pre-K. Units 1 to 11 are written day by day as drafts and none is approved yet (the full plans are for licensed centers); Unit 12 is being written. One room, mixed ages, the provider plus up to 3 assistants in the Hub.

With the kit

Planned design.
Planned design: the Futures Friends Learning Zones kit in our classroom (Booker's Reading Area added; not installed yet).
Photo: Futures Learning Center, Independence, Missouri
Trying counts here
Rewards
Friendship Stars

A star card from one of the friends for trying again, helping out, asking a question or finishing the puzzle a child nearly quit.

Exploring new foods
Food explorer talk

Look, smell, touch and describe new foods at the table. Tasting is always the child's choice, and nothing is charted or rewarded.

Community
Friday circle

On Friday the class sits together and names who showed the week's value. The news goes home to families.

Four zones, open all day
Booker's Reading Area
Early literacy, storytelling, listening, and the courage to try again.
Lumi's Calm Corner
Naming feelings, calming down, friendship and making room for everyone.
Zuri's Discovery Zone
Questions, nature, numbers, shapes and simple experiments.
Bop's Movement Zone
Movement, music, routines, clean-up and doing it myself.
Twos, pre-K and everyone in between
Age versions

Every activity has a simpler version for twos and a stretch for pre-K.

Observe and adapt

Learning Steps help teachers notice what each child is doing and what comes next.

Language support

Picture cards and key words for English learners.

Futures Include

Classroom adaptations and early intervention guidance, alongside the curriculum. The Futures Hub does not store IEP or IFSP goals or health records.

How far a piece has come. We use six words, always in this order: Written (A full draft exists. Nobody outside our team has reviewed it.) Reviewed (A second person on our team has read it and fixed what they found.) Approved (An early-childhood specialist has signed off on it.) Hosted (It is on the live Futures Hub, where a program can open it.) Released (It is in a published release that programs can receive.) Delivered (It has reached a program that uses it.)

The curriculum today. Units 1 to 11 are written as drafts on our private platform: Units 1 to 10 are merged, Unit 11 is in quality check and Unit 12 is being written. No early-childhood specialist has approved any unit yet, and none is hosted, released or delivered through the Futures Hub yet.

## The whole day, planned on purpose. Families get to see it.
https://dvolcore.github.io/futures-friends/whole-child

The whole-child day
THE WHOLE-CHILD DAY
The whole day, planned on purpose. Families get to see it.

A story, a snack, a stomp around the room, a rest, one question at pickup: planned together as one day. The same four friends and the same few words turn up from arrival to pickup, so each part backs up the others.

Try Bop at Home, free

FROM ARRIVAL TO PICKUP
One day, six steps.

Every step has a friend who looks after it, and a family can see all six.

1
Arrive

Two Taps

Check-in takes two taps, so the first minutes are for greeting the child.

Family Connection
2
Learn

Story + DO

A short story opens one idea. Then the screen goes off and hands-on play carries it.

Booker
3
Nourish

Meal or snack, and water

Regular meals stay familiar and complete. Color becomes a low-pressure way to explore food. Water is there all day.

Zuri
4
Move

Bop & Go!

Short movement moments through the day, with a water break at every transition.

Bop
5
Reset

Quiet Time

Notice, Breathe, Soften, Rest. Offered, never forced.

Lumi
6
Connect

Pickup prompt

"What's your one thing?" One question, one take-home card, one no-cost family challenge.

Family Connection

The point is not to add six separate programs. It is to design the day so the same characters, language and habits reinforce one another.

DAILY TARGETS, WITH SOURCES
What a day aims to deliver

These are defaults a center can edit, and every number shows where it comes from. Kansas and Missouri licensing rules layer on top as legal minimums: where a state rule is stricter, the state rule wins. Our screen limits are Futures Friends standards. Neither state limits screens.

Daily movement, outdoor, screen and sitting defaults by age band
AGE BAND ACTIVE PLAY OUTDOOR PLAY SCREEN SITTING OR RESTRAINED SOURCE

Twos
2 to under 3 60 to 90 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous play (MVPA). 60 to 90 minutes. None through age 2 (CFOC 2.2.0.3: “ages 2 and younger”). Awake confinement no more than 30 minutes. Sitting no more than 1 hour at a time. CFOC 3.1.3.1
(opens in a new tab)
 and 2.2.0.3 (4th ed.); WHO
(opens in a new tab)
; K.A.R. 28-4-440(f)

Preschool
3 to 5 90 to 120 minutes of MVPA. WHO: 180 minutes at any intensity, at least 60 of them MVPA. 60 to 90 minutes. Not more than 30 minutes a week in care by default, only for learning or movement and never at meals or snacks (the CDC early care and education standard for children 2 and older). Centers can lower it. No more than 1 hour at a time. CFOC 3.1.3.1
(opens in a new tab)
 and 2.2.0.3; WHO 2019
(opens in a new tab)
; CDC screen time limits in early care
(opens in a new tab)
State rules sit on top of these defaults

Your center’s state and program type decide which rules apply, and the daily plan shows the citation next to each one. These are summaries, not legal advice: your license and your state agency are the authority.

Kansas centers
At least 60 minutes outdoors once a child has been in care more than 4 hours.
Kansas homes: physical activity offered at least 1 hour a day.
Missouri
1 hour outdoors for full-day preschool and school-age children, weather permitting.
Preschoolers who do not sleep rest 30 to 60 minutes. Rest is required, and sleep never is.
No more than 4 hours between meals and snacks.
Both states
Water available at all times.
Food and rest are never used as punishment.
Neither state limits screen time. Our screen limits are Futures Friends standards, not legal requirements.

Missouri programs that are religious-exempt are excused from the daily-schedule rule. The defaults above still apply to them as Futures Friends standards, not as law.

How the day adds up
Activity can build up in bouts of 10 minutes or more.
Every child gets 2 to 3 outdoor occasions and 2 or more adult-led movement activities each day.
A gentle prompt appears when a room has gone too long without moving: after 30 minutes seated. One hour is the ceiling.
What we measure
Minutes, missions and outdoor occasions the day delivered.
Never a child's weight, BMI or calories, and never a ranking.
Sources
Caring for Our Children (CFOC)
(opens in a new tab)
, 4th edition (2019), standards 3.1.3.1 and 2.2.0.3 (PDF).
WHO guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years
(opens in a new tab)
.
LUMI OWNS BELONG AND RESET
Lumi's Quiet Time

Our reset routine for transitions, rest and noticing your body.

1
Notice
Speedy body or quiet body?
2
Breathe
A simple breathing ritual with Lumi.
3
Soften
Slower movement and a quieter voice.
4
Rest
A predictable transition into quiet or rest.
Children learn to notice how their body feels, then follow the same four steps every time.

Quiet Time is offered, never forced. Some state rules add a requirement: Missouri preschoolers who do not sleep must have a rest period of 30 to 60 minutes. In those rooms rest is required and sleep never is.

White and tan
Regular meals stay familiar and complete.
Color becomes a low-pressure exploration tool: “Can you find something green on your plate?”
Children can look, smell, touch or taste. Trying is the goal.
Cookbook, poster, placemat and take-home pages carry the idea home.
Words we use

“Want to explore it?” “What color is on your plate?” “You can look, smell or touch it. Tasting is up to you.”

Words we skip

“Good food” and “bad food.” “Clean your plate.” Dessert as a prize. Food is never a reward or a punishment.

See the menus and recipes on Eat the Rainbow.

: Bop & Go! between activities

Bop & Go! between activities A one-minute movement break: dance, freeze, try again.

An Outside Quest Zuri looks closely at the flowers. Outside, children find three things to notice.
The Quiet Time corner Lumi takes a slow, calm breath. Smell the flower, blow the candle.
HOW WE RUN IT
Promises, built into the software, the policy and the training

Whole-child means the child is never the thing being measured, ranked or managed.

Everyone moves, everyone belongs

Every Bop mission has an adapted version: seated or wheelchair, limited space, sensory-sensitive. Quiet Time is offered, never forced, except where a state rule requires a rest period.

Play is never a prize or a penalty

We never use movement, outdoor time or food as a reward or a punishment. The software has no place to record it, and teacher training says so.

Participation, not rankings

No leaderboards, no "most active" child, no comparing children. Families see their own child. Centers see rooms.

We count minutes, not bodies

We measure what the day delivered: minutes, missions and outdoor occasions. Never a child's weight, BMI, calories or a "healthy" label. Motor skills are noted only as observed milestones.

Screens fit the age

No episodes for children ages 2 and younger: songs, puppets and cards take their place. For preschoolers, not more than 30 minutes a week in care is the default, and a screen is the opening act, counted against that weekly cap.

Water and weather, with care

Water is available all day, with a prompt at every Bop & Go! transition. The forecast can suggest an indoor swap and shows why. The teacher decides.

Rest rules come first

Quiet Time follows the center's rest-time rules. Those rules always win.

Teachers move if they want to

Staff movement is opt-in and never tracked per person. Movement moments simply invite teachers to model.

Evidence-informed routines

We use recognized guidance, and plan a qualified review of health-related content before release. Futures Friends owns the characters, stories, rituals and delivery. We do not sell medical claims.

For families

Free movement activities you can do tonight, with an adapted version of every one.

SCHOOL READINESS
How Futures Friends supports every child

Adaptive software guesses what a child needs from clicks. Here the teacher watches the child, writes down what she saw and picks the next step, and the family gets the same note.

The learning loop
Observe and adapt
Learning Steps
Supports
Friendship Stars
Six steps, every day
1
Watch
A puppet story (episodes later)
2
Talk
Guided discussion
3
Do
Hands-on activity
4
Move
Physical play
5
Explore
Learning zones
6
Take home
Family connection
The teacher is the adaptive engine

Young children learn through relationships, not drills. The Futures Hub helps teachers see what each child needs next.

Observe

Teachers note what a child does and says in play and routines, tagged to a Learning Step for the child's age band, from twos to pre-K.

Describe in words

A level is a word (Emerging, Developing or Secure) backed by a dated note. Steps not seen yet show as "not yet observed", never as zero.

See what comes next

Every Learning Step names the next step to watch for and an idea to try at home.

Share with family

Families see what we saw, what's next and what to try at home. No scores, no rankings, no comparisons.

What teachers look for, from twos to pre-K

66 observable Learning Steps across seven areas of development. Each cites where it comes from, and each is checked against the official Missouri, Kansas and Head Start documents.

Age band Learning Steps Missouri (MELS 2021) Kansas (KELS 2024) Head Start (ELOF 2015)
Twos 24 to 35 months 19 17 of 19 matched 19 of 19 matched 18 of 19 matched
Threes 36 to 47 months 21 21 of 21 matched 21 of 21 matched 21 of 21 matched
Pre-K 48 months to kindergarten 26 23 of 26 matched 26 of 26 matched 24 of 26 matched
Sources
Sources on every step

Each step quotes its source: a CDC "Learn the Signs. Act Early." milestone, a Missouri example or a Kansas or Head Start indicator, checked word for word against the official documents.

Standards
Honest matching

Only codes found in the official documents are used. Where no standard truly matches, the step says "not matched" rather than guessing. Head Start has no separate arts or social studies goals; Missouri has no social studies domain.

Families
Not a test or screening

Learning Steps describe what children do in play. They are never used to label, rank or compare children, or to decide enrollment. If a family has a question, we point them to their doctor, Missouri First Steps or Kansas tiny-k.

Draft written from the cited documents and awaiting review by an early-childhood specialist. Sources: CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early. (2022 milestones); Missouri Early Learning Standards (DESE, 2021); Kansas Early Learning Standards (KSDE, 2024); Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework (2015). Accessed October 2026.

Mixed ages, one plan
Every age
Two-year-old and pre-K versions

Every activity has a simpler version for twos and a stretch for pre-K, so mixed groups learn together.

Language
English learners

Picture cards, gestures and key words for every Unit 1 day, in English with draft Spanish. Translated family letters are in development.

Social-emotional
Calm and belonging

Lumi's Calm Corner, breathing cards and positive guidance steps help children manage big feelings.

Language
Talk Time with Booker

Every story ends with open questions that invite vocabulary and back-and-forth conversation.

Special needs

Classroom adaptations and inclusion supports for children with disabilities and developmental delays.

Daily routines

Movement every day, the Eat the Rainbow menu and choking-safe food prep.

Explore Futures Include
Stars for effort, not points

No points on a screen. A child earns a star card for something real: trying again, helping a friend, asking a question, finishing the job.

Character achievement cards for each value

Welcome, teachers & providers
A sample lesson from the Futures Friends Academy (about 1.5 minutes). Ms. June is a teacher in our story world, not a member of our staff. Story-world animation.
Read the transcript
: Welcome, teachers & providers
THE LAW, IN PLAIN WORDS
Before any teacher is alone with your child

These are the minimums every licensed child care center must meet in Kansas and Missouri. They are not ours to choose. We list them so you know what to expect and what to ask.

STORY-WORLD ANIMATION
Principal Hazel
STORY-WORLD CHARACTER

First things first: before a grown-up teaches, the law asks who they are and whether they are ready.

1
Before the first shift

Before working, volunteering or being present

KANSAS
A background check that has cleared. Fingerprint-based for center staff and for volunteers counted in ratio, and covering every state the person lived in during the last 5 years. K.A.R. 28-4-125
MISSOURI
A comprehensive background check through the state: FBI fingerprints, sex offender registries and child abuse registries, including the Family Care Safety Registry, for every state lived in during the last 5 years. 5 CSR 25-600.020(1)
A new hire may start early on a qualifying fingerprint result only while supervised at all times by staff whose own check is complete. 5 CSR 25-600.020(2)(B)
2
Within 7 days

And before being left alone with children

KANSAS
A facility orientation: the licensing rules, emergency procedures, behavior and discipline policies, the daily schedule, each child's allergies and special needs, health and safety, and confidentiality. K.A.R. 28-4-428a(a)
MISSOURI
A documented facility orientation: a tour, the licensing rules, medication, illness and discipline practices, the needs of the children assigned, the emergency plan and how to report suspected abuse or neglect. 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(K)
Every caregiver reviews the licensing rules when they start. 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(H)
3
Within 30 days

In Kansas, also before sole responsibility for children

KANSAS
Health and safety training approved by the state, in 10 subject areas set by the state, including abuse and neglect, child development and supervision, illness and infection, food and allergy emergencies, building safety, emergency preparedness, hazardous materials, transportation and medication. K.A.R. 28-4-428a(b)
Pediatric first aid and pediatric CPR, with the skills shown in person to an instructor, and kept current. K.A.R. 28-4-428a(c)
A negative TB test or chest x-ray. K.A.R. 28-4-126(c)
MISSOURI
A medical exam report signed by a physician or a supervised nurse, with a TB risk assessment or a negative TB skin test. 5 CSR 25-500.122(1)
4
Every day

Whenever children are in care

KANSAS
At least one person with current pediatric first aid and CPR in every unit, at all times. K.A.R. 28-4-428a(c)(4)
Each staff member reports suspected abuse or neglect to the Kansas Department for Children and Families within 24 hours. K.A.R. 28-4-430(c)(2)
Medication is given only by staff who have completed medication administration training. K.A.R. 28-4-132(i)(1)
MISSOURI
Current first aid and CPR for at least one caregiver per 20 children of licensed capacity, and at least one on site whenever children are present. 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(T)
Suspected abuse or neglect is reported immediately to the Children's Division hotline, 1-800-392-3738. No one may investigate first or stand in the way of the report. RSMo 210.115; 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(J)
5
Every year

For as long as they work with children

KANSAS
16 clock hours of training approved by the state each licensure year, at least 4 of them in health and safety. Directors: 6 in program administration. Family home providers: 10 hours. K.A.R. 28-4-428a(e); 28-4-114a(d)(2)
An updated staff health status form, and practice of shelter-in-place and off-site relocation. K.A.R. 28-4-126(b); 28-4-128(a)
MISSOURI
12 clock hours of training approved by the state each calendar year, recorded in the state's MOPD system. Repeating a course in the same year earns no extra credit. 5 CSR 25-500.102(3)
A Family Care Safety Registry check on every staff member before the license anniversary. 5 CSR 25-500.052(2)(C)
6
Every 5 years

Background checks again

KANSAS
Fingerprints taken again when the Kansas Office of Early Childhood sends notice. KOEC background check guidance
MISSOURI
The full comprehensive background check repeated. 5 CSR 25-600.020(5)

Plain-language summaries of the Kansas rules in effect September 4, 2026 (K.A.R. 28-4, published by the Kansas Office of Early Childhood) and the Missouri rules (5 CSR 25-500 and 5 CSR 25-600, DESE Office of Childhood), checked October 4, 2026. They are not legal advice: the official text and your state agency are the authority. Family child care homes and Missouri religious-exempt programs follow different rules. Read the sources: Kansas center regulations
(opens in a new tab)
, Missouri 5 CSR 25-500
(opens in a new tab)
, Missouri 5 CSR 25-600
(opens in a new tab)
.

OUR STANDARD
Where our training goes further than the law

The states set the minimum. We designed our courses to add the six things below. They are in the course design now and will apply to our teachers as each course launches.

STORY-WORLD ANIMATION
Mr. Moss
STORY-WORLD CHARACTER

Knowing the rule is the start. Showing it, every day, is the standard.

Safety questions need 100%

Life-safety questions must be answered 100% correctly, whatever the overall score. A miss sends the teacher back to that lesson, then retests with a different question on the same point.

Life-safety topics include rest-time supervision, reporting abuse and neglect, and missing-child counts.

Seen doing it, in the room

Within 30 days of each course, the director (or a senior mentor teacher) watches the teacher at work and signs a short checklist for that course. A missed life-safety item starts a coaching plan.

The checklist is not counted as clock hours. It is proof the training reached the classroom.

Writing it down

Every course ends with one or two short written reflections, read by a coach. They are marked complete or not complete, never graded.

Example: "Walk through your room in your head. What one thing will you check differently at the next nap?"

Real time on task

No fast-forward and no skipping slides. An activity at least every 5 minutes means the course moves only when the teacher takes part, and the clock pauses when they step away.

Active time is logged for each part of the course.

Rest time for everyone who covers a nap

Our rest-time course is built for directors, teachers, floaters, substitutes and volunteers: anyone who may be in the room at nap time. It sets out our own practice for ages 2 to 5. Rest rules differ by state, so we confirm them with our licensing consultant.

Quiet Time is offered, never forced and never a punishment.

One named person signs every course

Each version of each course must be checked against the current rule text and signed by our Training Content Lead and Trainer of Record before teachers use it.

That role is not filled yet. Kansas and Missouri editions differ wherever the rules differ.

HOW TRAINING WORKS
Why scenario practice beats a video you can click through

A teacher can sit through a video and still not know what to do when a child will not settle at rest time. So every course is short lessons, constant practice and real decisions, then proof in the classroom.

STORY-WORLD ANIMATION
Ms. June
STORY-WORLD CHARACTER
The question behind the method

In our story world, I ask the children two questions. Good training asks the grown-ups the same two.

What do you notice? What do you wonder?
What do you notice?
What do you wonder?
1
Watch

A short video

Two to four minutes: a friend opener, a real-classroom demonstration filmed with family consent, or a scene acted by adults. No child is filmed in a staged unsafe scene.

2
Do

An activity every few minutes

Spot the hazards in a rest-area photo, put the reporting steps in order, choose what to do next. Progress waits for an answer.

3
Decide

Scenario questions

Drawn at random from a bank at least three times larger than the quiz, with feedback on every answer. 80% to pass, 3 attempts.

4
Master

Life-safety at 100%

Safety questions must be right every time. A miss means the lesson again and a new question.

5
Reflect

A coach reads it

One or two short written reflections, read and marked complete by a coach.

6
Show

On the job

The director observes in the classroom within 30 days and signs the course checklist.

A click-through video course compared with our course design
A CLICK-THROUGH VIDEO COURSE OUR COURSE DESIGN
Press play and walk away Progress stops until the teacher answers
One quiz at the very end Practice every few minutes, then a scenario check
A lucky guess can pass a safety question Safety questions need 100%
Done when the video ends Done when the director has seen it in the room

This design also follows the states' rules for online training. Missouri does not give clock-hour credit for self-study with a quiz or for pre-recorded webinars, and a self-paced course counts only on a learning platform the state has approved: one that blocks fast-forwarding, checks knowledge, requires interaction and tracks time present (DESE MOPD Trainer Guide
(opens in a new tab)
; DESE Asynchronous Training Overview
(opens in a new tab)
, Oct. 2025). Our platform has not been approved yet. Pediatric first aid and CPR are taught in person by an outside partner, never online.

THE PILOT COURSE, IN DEVELOPMENT
Rest Time and Lumi's Quiet Time

The first course we are building. Rest time is when one adult must see and hear every child, so we start there. If this course meets the bar, the format does.

LENGTH
1.5
hours
SHORT VIDEOS
13
of 2 to 4 minutes
ACTIVITIES
16
along the way
SAFETY CHECKPOINT
4
questions at minute 55, 100% to go on
FINAL CHECK
8
questions from a bank of 28, 16 of them life-safety
REFLECTIONS
2
read by a coach
What teachers practice
Set up the rest area: each child on their own labeled cot or mat, cots spaced apart, with clear walkways to every exit.
Check every cot: the child's own labeled bedding, cords kept away, and no food, drink or hazard objects on the cot. Shoes off and stored.
Keep every resting child in sight and in hearing, with lighting that lets you see each child.
After the rest period, give children who do not sleep a quiet activity so the others can keep resting.
Lead Lumi's Quiet Time (Notice, Breathe, Soften, Rest) for twos through pre-K: offered, never forced, never a punishment, and within each state's rest rule.
What the director checks in the room, within 30 days
Each child on their own labeled cot or mat
Cots or mats spaced apart, with clear walkways
Each child's own labeled bedding
Lighting that lets staff see each child
Staff placed to see and hear every resting child
No equipment that blocks seeing or hearing
No food, drink or hazard objects on cots
Shoes off and stored, cords kept away
Quiet activities ready for children who do not sleep after the rest period
Quiet Time led with the four steps
Children who do not sleep get a quiet activity, per the state rule
Rest is never used as punishment

This course is a design (draft 0.1). It has not yet been reviewed by our trainer of record or by either state. This is the program's own rest-time practice for ages 2 to 5. Confirm the exact rest rules with your licensing consultant. Quiet Time is for twos through pre-K.

HOW WE VERIFY MASTERY
What "complete" means

When a course is live, a teacher's record for it is complete only when every line below is true.

Every video segment watched, with no skipping
Every activity answered
Life-safety questions: 100%
Overall knowledge check: 80% or higher, within 3 attempts
Reflections read and marked complete by a coach
Active time logged for each part, with idle time paused
Director's on-the-job checklist signed within 30 days

The completion certificate shows the course code, version and hours. State credit appears on it only after Kansas (through Cape, the state's training registry) or Missouri (through the MOPD system) has approved the course and recorded the completion.

STORY-WORLD ANIMATION
Ms. Fern
STORY-WORLD CHARACTER

If a grown-up misses a safety question, they go back and learn it again. That is not a failure. That is the point.

EVERY YEAR AFTER
Training comes round every year

The states require training every year. Our draft catalog plans it by role, so the minimum is met without repeating a course.

The hours, planned by role
Kansas centers: 16 hours a licensure year, at least 4 in health and safety. Kansas homes: 10.
Missouri: 12 hours a calendar year.
Each plan in our draft catalog meets the state minimum without repeating a course in the same year.
A needs check every year
In Kansas, the director must assess each teacher's training needs every licensure year (K.A.R. 28-4-428a(e)(2)).
Every new course brings its own director checklist.
Renewals that matter
Pediatric first aid and CPR kept current, in person.

A Missouri center teacher

From our draft catalog. These courses are in development, and their hours count toward Missouri's 12 only after the state approves each one.

FOR FAMILIES
What you can ask to see

Any licensed program should be able to answer these questions. Ask us too.

The written rest-time policy

Ask to see the center's rest-time plan: where children rest, how adults see and hear them, and what children do if they do not sleep. Rules differ by state, so confirm with your licensing consultant.

The program's own practice

The emergency plan

Kansas programs review it with parents and with staff every year: fire, weather, a missing child, lockdown, where children go and how families are reunited.

K.A.R. 28-4-128(a)

Who has current first aid and CPR today

Ask how the program makes sure someone with current pediatric first aid and CPR is with your child's group all day.

K.A.R. 28-4-428a(c); 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(T)

Whether each teacher in the room has finished orientation and health and safety training

Programs keep these records in each person's file. Expect a yes or no, not the personal file: background check results stay confidential.

K.A.R. 28-4-428a(f); 5 CSR 25-500.102(1)(N)

How abuse or neglect is reported

Every staff member reports directly. In Missouri that means calling the Children's Division hotline right away; no one may investigate first.

RSMo 210.115

Our course outlines, once a course is live

Ask to see the course outline, its life-safety topics and the director checklist. They are the same for every teacher who takes the course.

Our policy

Where we are today

We are preparing our courses for state review. Nothing on this page is approved by Kansas or Missouri yet, and we will say so plainly until it is.

Done

; in Missouri, through DESE's MOPD system. Pediatric first aid and CPR always come from an in-person provider.

Room pictures are design renderings of how the zones can look.

Delivered today:
nothing yet.
Starts:
When ordering opens and each item is made; posters and zone signs are draft art, not print-ready.
Recurring billing:
None: one-time orders.

What ships

Print items by parcel. Rugs, mats and fences by freight, quoted by ZIP code before you pay. Plush when it opens.

Lead times

Made-to-order items are timed by the maker. You get the date in writing before any charge.

Made for licensing

Our friends and designs are made for licensed programs. The kits match what is on your walls in training.

A real person

Call (816) 988-5661 or send a request. We answer within two business days.

Measure the room, then order.

The Room Planner checks square feet per child, exits and sight lines for your space, then builds a parts list you can send us. It takes about ten minutes.

Open the Room Planner
See the Learning Zones Kit
A 20 x 25 ft classroom, to scale.
Before you order
Children’s Product Certificate
Children’s items ship only with a CPSIA Children’s Product Certificate and a tracking label.
Small parts, under 3
Items that are not tested for children under 3 carry a small-parts warning.
Sales tax
We collect Missouri and Kansas sales tax on taxable orders. Tax-exempt orders need a certificate.
Freight for rugs
Rugs, mats and fence panels ship by freight. The carrier cost is quoted by ZIP code before you pay.
Returns
Draft
Returns and refunds policy: Draft, owner and counsel to confirm.
Terms of sale
Draft
Terms of sale: Draft, owner and counsel to confirm.
Order privacy
Order details are used to fill your order and are never sold. Children’s data is not collected.

Shopping for home? The Kids’ Shop has shirts, hoodies and backpacks, plush friends, carpets, posters and free activity pages.

Visit the Kids’ Shop

## The Learning Zones Kit
https://dvolcore.github.io/futures-friends/room-kit

Home
/
For centers & programs
/
Program options
/
Learning Zones Kit
For centers, home daycares and church programs
The Learning Zones Kit

Learn. Move. Explore. Belong.

Each friend gets a space in your room: a carpet, a low fence, a sign, a poster and a friend puppet. A chime and a friend’s voice tell children where to go next, and a paw-print path on the floor takes them there. It works in a 12 x 14 ft home daycare, a center classroom, or a church hall that is cleared by Sunday.

Ages 2 to 5
Home, center and church layouts
Fences 22 to 24 in: adults see every zone
English and Spanish signs
Request a quote
See the room layouts
Booker
Booker’s Reading Area
Lumi
Lumi’s Calm Corner
Zuri
Zuri’s Discovery Zone
Bop
Bop’s Movement Zone

Story-world characters

Designed for real corners.

Booker’s reading corner and Lumi’s calm corner, each marked by its own carpet and poster.

The five zones
One space per friend, plus the circle they share

The zone names match the curriculum, the staff training and the Futures Hub, so children, teachers and families use the same words. Each friend’s colour runs through the mat, the fence, the sign and the path.

Friends Circle

Gold rim, all four friends · Shared by everyone

Where the day starts and ends: hello, talking together, watching the week’s short episode together, and goodbye. Every floor path in the room starts here.

8 ft round rug (6 ft at home)
30 sit spots
Hand chime
Six friend cue cards
Path: Gold sit spots

Booker, Lumi, Zuri and Bop are story-world characters.

Booker’s Reading Area

Blue · Learn + Smile

A calm space for books, letters and telling stories back. Quiet zones sit away from the door and from active play.

Blue zone mat
Zone sign and poster
Booker stick puppet
Picture + word bin labels
Path: Book prints
Hear Booker’s cue

Booker is a story-world character.

Lumi’s Calm Corner

Pink · Belong + Reset

A soft place a child chooses when feelings get big, with family photos close by. Always a choice, never a time-out, and always in an adult’s line of sight.

Pink zone mat
Zone sign and poster
Lumi stick puppet
Calm-down picture cards
Path: Heart-shaped petals
Hear Lumi’s cue

Lumi is a story-world character.

Zuri’s Discovery Zone

Green · Explore + Nourish

Sorting, measuring, sensory bins, nature finds and food exploring. It sits next to the sink, the tables and the Eat the Rainbow wall.

Green zone mat
Zone sign and poster
Zuri stick puppet
Small-parts card for rooms with 2s
Path: Turtle tracks
Hear Zuri’s cue

Zuri is a story-world character.

Bop’s Movement Zone

Purple · Move + Outside

Open floor for dancing, balancing, music and pretend play, and the door to outside. In a small home room, Bop’s zone shares the Friends Circle.

Purple zone mat
Zone sign and poster
Bop stick puppet
Bop & Go spot line

How children move
The same cue, every transition

Young children follow routines they can see and hear. Every Futures Friends room uses one sequence, so children learn it in the first week and start moving on their own.

1
The chime
One soft tone from the teacher’s hand chime means “listen.”
2
The friend card
The teacher holds up a friend’s cue card: who is calling.
3
The friend’s voice
That friend’s own voice line plays, the same voice children hear in the videos.
4
The paw-print path
Children follow that friend’s prints on the floor, from the circle to the zone’s doorway.
5
The mat
Arriving means sitting on the friend’s mat. The chime brings everyone back to the circle.
Try it: hear a friend call

Plush friends are in development and must pass toy-safety testing first. Kits are planned to include printed friend stick puppets, and the plush follow once they pass.

The Friend Fence
Low enough to see over, steady enough to stay put

Licensing asks that children are supervised by sight and sound at all times. So the fence marks a space for children without hiding them from adults. This is our proposed spec; a prototype must pass a tip test before any panel is sold.

Height
22 to 24 in, never above 30 in. A seated adult sees a sitting child.
See-through top
The upper half of every panel is mesh or clear, so no zone is hidden.
Anti-tip
Wide weighted feet or a self-standing fold; it must stay upright under a sideways push at the top edge.
Nothing to climb
No footholds, no openings a head could slip through, soft fabric hinges with no pinch points.
Soft edges
Rounded corners and top edge, no exposed hardware.
Doorways
Two panels per zone leave a 30 to 36 in opening, wide enough for a wheelchair or walker.
Washable
A removable, machine-washable printed sleeve; the core wipes clean.
22–24 in
36 in panel
seated adult’s eye line
see-through top
Proposed panel. Never above 30 in.

Built safe
What we check before anything ships
Flammability-tested rugs
Every rug and mat design needs a federal flammability report (16 CFR 1630 or 1631) and a Children’s Product Certificate before it ships.
Toy-safety-tested plush
Plush ship only after testing to the U.S. toy standard (ASTM F963): embroidered faces, no small parts. Until then, printed puppets.
Sightlines first
Fences stay 22 to 24 in with see-through tops, every plan marks the adult positions, and Lumi’s Calm Corner is always in view.
Washable mats where your state requires them
Some states bar carpet in rooms for the youngest children (Missouri does, 5 CSR 25-500.082). Those rooms get washable mats laundered daily.
Square feet per child
Each layout is checked against your licensed space: Missouri 35 sq ft per child, Kansas centers 28, Kansas homes 25.
Clear exits
Exit paths stay 36 in clear, nothing sits in a door swing, and wall art is planned under the 20 percent fire-code cap.

Every zone also has an icon and a word, not only a colour, and 36 in routes between zones for wheelchairs and walkers. Family updates describe the class’s day, never a child’s location.

HOW SUPPORT WORKS
Hours, urgent help and what is included
Support hours

Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM Central.

Proposed, owner to confirm

We answer within one business day: (816) 988-5661, info@futureslearningcenter.com.

Something urgent?

Call the main line and say it is urgent. A child in danger or a medical emergency: call 911 first. Suspected abuse or neglect: call your state’s hotline. Those are never a Futures Friends support ticket.

Three kinds of help
Kind What it covers Cost
Technical help Sign-in, the Hub, the Teacher Portal, printing. Included for every member. Included
Classroom coaching How a lesson ran, a room set-up, a child who needs a different approach (no child’s private details by email). Monthly office hours and your coordinator calls. Included. Included
Extra consulting More sessions for your staff or a day on site: a live training session (90 minutes, up to 15 staff) or an on-site launch day in the Kansas City metro. Priced on the Pricing page. Extra
The launch sequence
1
Set-up Week 0

Your rooms, staff list and sign-ins; the welcome box arrives as pieces are made.

2
Staff orientation Week 1

A live session for your team: the friends, the daily rhythm, Unit 1.

3
First classroom use Week 2

Teach the first days. A coordinator checks in at the end of the week.

4
Family introduction Week 3

A letter home, Futures at Home for every family and a family night if you want one.

5
30-day review Day 30

What worked, what to change, what next month brings.

When a teacher leaves

A replacement starts with your state’s required checks and orientation, then shadows a teacher for the first days. Level 1 Foundations in the Academy follows as part of the monthly fee once its courses are ready. Your coordinator can join a catch-up call.

Launching with pilot
Church volunteers

A 20-minute orientation for rotating volunteers and a one-page handover sheet for each session. See how churches run Futures Friends.

FUNDING HELP
Funding your program may qualify for

CACFP, child care subsidy, grants and the 45F tax credit: what each one pays, what to check first and where to start. If you would rather not do the paperwork, we will do it for a flat fee.

Program What it pays Check before you apply Next step
CACFP (Missouri DHSS) Cash for each qualifying meal and snack Check current rules Apply through CNPWeb; collect income forms from every family
Child care subsidy (DESE) Part of tuition for eligible families Check enrollment status Keep your provider contract current
DESE Innovation grants Start-up and expansion funds Check for open rounds Prepare a grant-ready file now
Imagination Library Free monthly books under age 5 Only where a local program is taking sign-ups Run the Futures lending library
Employer 45F credit Federal credit for employer child care support Federal credit; ask your tax advisor Use the employer pitch in the marketing kit
Done for you
CACFP setup

We prepare your application, forms and records system. Center $950, home $250.

Done for you
Monthly compliance

Claim review and records check each month. Center $195, home $49.

Done for you
Grant writing

A complete application for a flat fee, never a percentage. Center $1,500, home $450.
